short: One of Rome's grandest aqueducts, begun by Caligula and finished by the emperor it was named for.
full:
Caligula started the Aqua Claudia in 38 CE, judging Rome's seven existing aqueducts insufficient for the growing city's demand. Claudius, who had succeeded him after the assassination of 41 CE, completed the works in 52 CE and gave the aqueduct his name. It ran roughly 69 kilometres from springs in the Anio valley to Rome, most of it underground, before its final approach carried it into the city on a tall arcade of concrete-and-stone piers, a stretch of which still stands near the later Porta Maggiore.

The Aqua Claudia and the Anio Novus, built alongside it on the same route, together delivered a large share of Rome's water supply and fed some of the city's principal fountains and the Caelian Hill. Later emperors, notably Vespasian and Titus, had to repair sections that had already fallen into disrepair within a few decades, a reminder of how much continuous maintenance the aqueduct system demanded to keep a million-strong city supplied.
